senses.gloss:
punarādheya
(‘reinstallation [of Vedic fires]’)
------------------------------------------
During the Vedic and the epic periods, many dvijas (the twice-born class or the members of the first three varṇas) used to establish the Vedic fires for regular oblations and special sacrifices.
If the Vedic fires got extinguished due to certain contingencies like illness, loss of wealth, death of near and dear ones or harassment by enemies or even by accident, they could be rekindled or reinstated. This process was known as पुनराधेय or punarādhāna.
The procedure was essentially the same as for अग्न्याधान (See AGNYĀDHĀNA for details.), but with a few differences like feeding the fire with कुश grass (Poa cynosuroides) instead of समिध् (fuel sticks) and offerings to अग्नि alone, instead of अग्नि and सोम.
In case both the गार्हपत्य and the आहवनीय fires had been extinguished, पुनराधेय was considered a प्रायश्चित्त or expiation for the sin also.

punarjanma
(‘rebirth’)
------------------------------------------
The theory of कर्म and पुनर्जन्म or rebirth, is a basic tenet of हिन्दुइस्म्. The principle behind it is, ‘As you sow, so you reap’. पुनर्जन्म is regulated by प्रारब्धकर्म. See PRĀRABDHAKARMA for details.
Hinduism accepts the regression of a सोउल् into animal bodies, but only to exhaust the bad karmas, before being born again in a human body.

Punarvasu
(‘fresh wealth’ or ‘new growth’)
------------------------------------------
This is the seventh out of the twenty-seven nakṣatras (constellation of स्तर्स्) accepted by Hindu almanacs and astrologers. The स्तर्स् of this नक्षत्र are alpha and beta Geminorum.
Caula or tonsure for a male child is to be done in the third year after birth, on a day associated with this नक्षत्र.
It is considered auspicious for other rites also like उपनयन and मर्रिअगे.

punarbhū
(‘[a woman who has] married again’)
------------------------------------------
Remarriage of widows seems to have been permitted in the ancient days under certain conditions. Such a woman was known as ‘punarbhū’.
A पुनर्भू was of three kinds:
A maiden whose मर्रिअगे was not consummated and whose husband died suddenly.
A woman accused of अदुल्तेर्य् but returned to her parents who gave her in मर्रिअगे to another man.
A widow remarried to a close relative of her husband. (Whether she was childless or not, is not clear in this case.)
A married woman was permitted to remarry by some धर्मशास्त्रस् under the following conditions:
When a husband dies very early or is lost or unheard of for a long time; if he becomes a saṁnyāsin (monk); if he is impotent or suffering from incurable diseases or a sinner.
Though remarriage was perhaps permitted in the earliest age (vide Ṛgveda 10.18.7 and 8; Atharvaveda 5.17.8 and 9), during the later period, more stringent rules were imposed for the same. Some of the smṛtis even frowned upon the custom (vide Manusmṛti 9.47; 8.226). Insistence on chastity and the social implications like maidens not getting good husbands may be one of the reasons for the hardening of this stand.
